verses.text: Zeus thundered with a harsh and mighty crash, and all around the earth
rang terribly, as did the wide sky above,
the sea, the streams of Oceanus, and Tartarus beneath the earth.
Great Olympus shook beneath the immortal feet
of the king as he sprang into action, and the earth groaned.
Heat from both fighters gripped the violet-dark sea,
from thunder and lightning, from the monster's fire,
from fiery blasts of wind and the blazing thunderbolt.
All the earth boiled, and the sky and sea.
Long waves raged around the shores on every side
under the force of the immortals, and the shaking would not stop.
Hades trembled, ruler of the dead below,
and so did the Titans deep in Tartarus, gathered around Cronus,
at the endless roar and the terrible fighting.
Then Zeus gathered all his strength and took up his weapons,
thunder, lightning, and the smoking thunderbolt.
He leaped from Olympus and struck, scorching all
the monstrous heads of the terrifying creature.
When Zeus had beaten him down with blow after blow,
Typhoeus fell, his limbs powerless, and the vast earth groaned.
Flame rushed from the thunderstruck lord Typhoeus
in the mountain's dark and rugged valleys,
as he lay stricken. A great stretch of the vast earth burned
in the tremendous heat and melted like tin
heated by skilled young men in well-pierced crucibles,
or like iron, the strongest metal of all,
which yields to blazing fire in mountain valleys
and melts in the sacred earth beneath Hephaestus's hands.
So the earth melted in the glare of the burning fire.
In bitter anger, Zeus hurled Typhoeus into wide Tartarus.
From Typhoeus comes the force of the moisture-laden winds,
except for Notus, Boreas, and sky-clearing Zephyrus.
These are born of the gods, a great help to mortals,
but the others blow across the sea as reckless gusts.
They fall upon the misty sea
and rage in vicious storms, bringing great suffering to mortals.
Now one wind blows, now another; they scatter ships
and kill sailors. There is no defense against this harm
for people who meet these winds at sea.
These winds also sweep across the boundless, flowering earth
and ruin the lovely work of earth-born people,
filling the land with dust and a dreadful uproar.
When the blessed gods had brought their struggle to an end
and settled by force their dispute with the Titans over honors,
they urged Zeus to be king and ruler,
the far-seeing god of Olympus, on Gaia's advice,
to reign over the immortals. Zeus shared out their honors among them.
Zeus, king of the gods, made Metis his first wife.
She knew more than any other god or mortal.
But when Metis was about to give birth to bright-eyed Athena,
Zeus cunningly deceived her mind
with coaxing words and swallowed her into his belly,
on the advice of Gaia and starry Uranus.
They had advised him to do this so that no one else
would hold Zeus's royal place among the everlasting gods.
For Metis was destined to bear children of great wisdom:
first a daughter, bright-eyed Athena, called Tritogeneia,
equal to her father in strength and wise judgment.
Then Metis was to bear a son, a king of gods and humans,
with a fierce and mighty heart.
But before that, Zeus swallowed Metis into his belly,
so that the goddess could advise him on good and evil.
